lesson.summary: In a parallel circuit every branch gets the **full source voltage**, and the **current splits up** across however many paths are available.
lesson.content:
## Parallel Circuits: Multiple Paths

> **Core Concept:** In a parallel circuit every branch gets the **full source voltage**, and the **current splits up** across however many paths are available.

### Why It Matters
- Most real devices in your house (lights, outlets, appliances) are wired in parallel, not series, so you need this model to understand how normal wiring actually behaves.
- Without understanding parallel paths, it's confusing why unplugging one lamp doesn't turn off every other lamp in the house.
- Parallel circuits explain why adding more branches to a circuit can pull more total current from the source, even though each branch's own resistance never changed.

### Intuitive Analogy
Picture a water tower feeding several separate hoses, each with its own
nozzle. Every hose gets the same water pressure straight from the tower
(voltage), since they all connect to the same source independently. But the
total water leaving the tower (current) is the sum of whatever flows out of
each individual hose. Pinch one hose and only that hose's flow drops, the
others keep running exactly as before.


### Key Engineering Principles
- A parallel circuit has more than one path, each component (or branch) connects directly across the same two points, usually called the top rail and bottom rail in a schematic.
- **Voltage is identical** across every branch in parallel. Each branch independently 'sees' the full source voltage, because voltage is a property between two shared points, and every branch shares those exact same two points.
- **Current, on the other hand, divides**. Each branch draws its own current based on its own resistance and Ohm's law, and those individual branch currents add up to the total current the source has to supply.
- Worked example: a 9V source feeding three branches of 100Ω, 220Ω, and 330Ω. Each branch sees the full 9V, so branch currents are roughly 90mA, 41mA, and 27mA. The source itself has to supply all three added together, about 158mA total.
- Total resistance in parallel is found with the **reciprocal formula**: 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 and so on. For just two resistors there's a shortcut, R_total = (R1 x R2) / (R1 + R2).
- ==Combined resistance in parallel is always lower than the smallest individual branch resistance==, never higher. In the worked example above, 1/100 + 1/220 + 1/330 works out to a total resistance of roughly 57Ω, lower than even the smallest 100Ω branch alone.
- Adding more parallel branches always lowers the total resistance of the circuit further and increases the total current the source must supply, even though no single branch's own resistance changed at all. This is why plugging too many devices into one outlet can trip a breaker, more parallel paths means more total current demand.
- If one branch breaks open, the other branches keep working normally, since each has its own independent path back to the source. This is exactly why one burnt-out light bulb at home doesn't take down every other outlet in the room.
- A special, easy-to-remember case: two equal resistors in parallel always combine to exactly half the value of either one alone. Two 100Ω resistors in parallel give 50Ω total, regardless of what the rest of the circuit looks like.
- Most household wiring, and most breadboard prototypes with more than one LED, use parallel branches for exactly this reason, each device needs the same full voltage and should keep working independently of whatever else is plugged in.

topics.title: Potentiometers: Resistance You Can Turn
topics.description: A **potentiometer** is a resistor whose value you can change by hand, using a sliding **wiper** contact to tap off a variable amount of resistance or voltage.

lesson.summary: A **potentiometer** is a resistor whose value you can change by hand, using a sliding **wiper** contact to tap off a variable amount of resistance or voltage.
lesson.content:
## Potentiometers: Resistance You Can Turn

> **Core Concept:** A **potentiometer** is a resistor whose value you can change by hand, using a sliding **wiper** contact to tap off a variable amount of resistance or voltage.

### Why It Matters
- Fixed resistors are great when a value is known ahead of time, but plenty of real controls (volume, brightness, speed) need to be **adjustable** by a person.
- Building an adjustable control from scratch with switches and multiple resistors would be clunky and imprecise compared to a smooth turn or slide.
- It helps to know whether a knob is acting as a **variable resistor** or as a **voltage divider**, since they get wired differently.

### Intuitive Analogy
A potentiometer is like a long resistive ramp with a movable rider standing
on it. The full ramp, end to end, is a fixed length (fixed total
resistance). Slide the rider toward one end, and the distance from the
rider to that end shrinks. The rider's position doesn't change the ramp
itself, it just changes how much of it you're measuring or tapping into at
that moment.


### Key Engineering Principles
- A potentiometer has a strip of resistive material with two fixed end terminals, and a third terminal attached to a **wiper** that slides or rotates along that strip.
- The **full resistance** between the two end terminals never changes, it's fixed by the part itself, like a 10k ohm potentiometer.
- The resistance between the wiper and either end terminal does change as you turn or slide it, that's the adjustable part.
- Used with just two terminals (one end plus the wiper), it acts as a simple **variable resistor**, useful for things like adjusting a motor's speed or an LED's brightness.
- Used with all three terminals, it acts as a **voltage divider**, the wiper taps off a fraction of the voltage across the full strip depending on its position, which is exactly how a volume knob works.
- A dimmer switch and a volume knob are both potentiometers under the hood, turning the knob physically moves the wiper along the resistive strip.
- Cheap potentiometers can get ==noisy or scratchy== over years of use as the wiper contact wears down, that's the scratchy sound an old volume knob sometimes makes.
- Potentiometers come in **linear taper** (resistance changes evenly as you turn it) and **logarithmic (audio) taper** (resistance changes more slowly at first then faster). Audio volume controls use log taper because human hearing perceives loudness logarithmically, a linear taper volume knob feels like all the change happens in the last few degrees of turn.
- A **trimmer potentiometer**, or trimpot, is a small, often screwdriver-adjusted version meant to be set once during calibration and rarely touched again, distinct from a knob meant for regular user adjustment.
- **Digital potentiometers** exist too, a chip that mimics a mechanical potentiometer's behavior electronically, controlled by digital signals instead of a physical wiper, useful when a microcontroller needs to adjust a resistance in code.

topics.title: Project: The Classic Blinking LED
topics.description: Blinking an LED with **code**, not a switch, is the moment a circuit stops being static wiring and becomes a program.

lesson.summary: Blinking an LED with **code**, not a switch, is the moment a circuit stops being static wiring and becomes a program.
lesson.content:
## Project: The Classic Blinking LED

> **Core Concept:** Blinking an LED with **code**, not a switch, is the moment a circuit stops being static wiring and becomes a program.

### Why It Matters
- Every electronics tutorial starts here for a reason: it's the smallest possible loop from code to a visible, physical result.
- It forces you to actually wire a real component (LED plus resistor) correctly, not just simulate one.
- It proves your whole toolchain works: writing code, uploading it, and having the board run it, before you try anything harder.

### Intuitive Analogy
Think of this project like learning to say your first word after years of only
listening. You already know a microcontroller can run code and an LED can
light up, but until you make one actually control the other, it's all
theory. Blinking an LED is the first sentence: short, simple, and proof that
the connection between your code and the real world actually works.


### Key Engineering Principles
- Parts needed: one LED, one **resistor** (around 220 ohm), a few jumper wires, and a breadboard, plus your microcontroller board.
- Wiring: connect a digital output pin to the resistor, the resistor to the LED's longer leg (anode), and the LED's shorter leg (cathode) to ground.
- The resistor is ==not optional==, it protects the LED from pulling more current than it can survive straight off the pin, since a bare pin driven HIGH behaves like a small, stiff voltage source with almost no built-in current limiting.
- In code, **pinMode()** sets that digital pin as OUTPUT before anything else happens, inside setup(). setup() itself only runs once, right after the board powers on or resets, which is exactly why one-time configuration belongs there and nowhere else.
- The **loop()** function then repeats forever: turn the pin HIGH (LED on), wait, turn it LOW (LED off), wait, and repeat. Nothing about loop() ever pauses permanently, it just keeps re-running from the top for as long as the board has power.
- **digitalWrite()** is the command that actually sets a pin's voltage, HIGH drives it to the board's logic voltage (5V on most Arduino Uno boards, 3.3V on many newer boards), LOW drives it to 0V.
- The **delay()** values, in milliseconds, are what you tune to make the blink faster or slower. delay() also ==fully pauses the program==, so nothing else in loop() can happen while it's counting down, a detail that matters a lot once a project needs to do more than one thing at once.
- A breadboard's rows are internally connected in short strips, and the LED, resistor, and jumper wires only form a working circuit if they share the right rows, a component in the wrong row is electrically disconnected even though it looks plugged in.
- Current always needs a **complete loop** back to the source. In this project that loop is: pin, through the resistor, through the LED, into GND, and back into the board internally to the same power supply that drives the pin.

topics.title: Project: Button-Controlled LED
topics.description: Adding a **button** turns your circuit from something that just runs on its own into something that reacts to the outside world.

lesson.summary: Adding a **button** turns your circuit from something that just runs on its own into something that reacts to the outside world.
lesson.content:
## Project: Button-Controlled LED

> **Core Concept:** Adding a **button** turns your circuit from something that just runs on its own into something that reacts to the outside world.

### Why It Matters
- Every interesting device eventually needs to respond to a human action, and a pushbutton is the simplest possible input to start with.
- This project introduces **digitalRead()**, the input counterpart to the digitalWrite() you already used for the LED.
- It also introduces **pull-down resistors**, a small wiring detail that trips up almost every beginner exactly once.

### Intuitive Analogy
If the blinking LED project was your microcontroller talking, this one is
it listening. A pushbutton is like a doorbell: nothing happens until
someone presses it, and the microcontroller's whole job here is to keep
checking, over and over, whether that press has happened yet.


### Key Engineering Principles
- Parts needed: one LED, one resistor for the LED, one pushbutton, one pull-down resistor (around 10k ohm) for the button, jumper wires, breadboard.
- LED wiring stays the same as the blinking LED project: output pin, resistor, LED anode, LED cathode to ground.
- Button wiring: one side of the button to 5V, the other side to both an input pin and, through the pull-down resistor, to ground.
- The pull-down resistor matters because without it, an unpressed button leaves the input pin ==floating==, reading randomly instead of a clean LOW, since nothing is actively holding that pin at a known voltage.
- In code, pinMode() sets the button pin as **INPUT** and the LED pin as **OUTPUT**. Getting these swapped, or leaving one as the board's default, is a common source of a project that seems to do nothing.
- loop() reads the button pin with digitalRead(), and if it's HIGH (pressed), writes the LED pin HIGH, otherwise writes it LOW.
- A **pull-up resistor** is the mirror image of a pull-down: it wires the input pin to 5V by default and the button pulls it to ground when pressed, meaning the logic in code flips, pressed reads LOW instead of HIGH. Many boards even have this built in as INPUT_PULLUP, saving a physical resistor.
- A pushbutton's four legs are usually two internally connected pairs, so two legs are always electrically joined to each other no matter what, and pressing the button only bridges those two separate pairs together.
- Mechanical switches like this one can ==bounce==, very briefly flickering between HIGH and LOW several times within a few milliseconds of being pressed or released, before settling. Simple projects like this one usually don't notice, but it becomes important once code needs to count individual presses.

topics.title: Project: A WiFi-Controlled Switch
topics.description: A **relay** lets a low-power microcontroller safely switch a household-power device on and off, and adding WiFi lets you trigger that relay from anywhere.

lesson.summary: A **relay** lets a low-power microcontroller safely switch a household-power device on and off, and adding WiFi lets you trigger that relay from anywhere.
lesson.content:
## Project: A WiFi-Controlled Switch

> **Core Concept:** A **relay** lets a low-power microcontroller safely switch a household-power device on and off, and adding WiFi lets you trigger that relay from anywhere.

### Why It Matters
- A microcontroller's GPIO pins can only safely handle a tiny amount of current, nowhere near what a lamp or appliance actually draws.
- Household devices often run on much higher voltage than a microcontroller's logic level, directly wiring them together would fry the board or worse.
- You want to flip that switch from your phone across the room or across the world, not walk over and flip it by hand every time.

### Intuitive Analogy
Think of a relay as a tiny, electrically-controlled hand. Your
microcontroller doesn't touch the dangerous, high-power switch directly,
instead it sends a small, safe signal that tells the relay's hand to press
the real switch on your behalf. The microcontroller stays safely on the
low-power side the whole time, it never has to touch the risky wiring
itself.


### Key Engineering Principles
- A relay is an electrically controlled switch, a small signal from the microcontroller energizes a coil inside it, which physically closes a separate, isolated switch.
- That separate switch can safely carry much higher voltage and current than the microcontroller pin ever could, because the two sides are **electrically isolated** from each other, there is no shared wire between control and load.
- The microcontroller only ever touches the low-power control side of the relay, never the high-power side, which keeps the whole setup much safer.
- Most GPIO pins can't supply enough current to energize a relay coil directly, so a small transistor usually sits between the pin and the coil, acting as an amplifier just for that switching current.
- A relay coil is an inductor, and inductors resist sudden changes in current, when the coil switches off, it can briefly generate a voltage spike backward through the circuit. A **flyback diode** wired across the coil gives that spike a safe path to dissipate instead of damaging the transistor.
- Two relay contact types matter: **normally open**, which stays disconnected until energized, and **normally closed**, which stays connected until energized. A lamp switch is almost always wired to the normally open contacts.
- Adding WiFi means the microcontroller can receive a command from your phone or a cloud service, then translate that command into simply setting a GPIO pin high or low.
- The full loop is: you tap a button in an app, that request travels to the board over WiFi, the board sets a pin, the relay clicks, the device turns on or off.
- ==Any relay-switched device on household mains voltage should be wired by, or with the direct supervision of, someone experienced with mains wiring==, the low-voltage control side is forgiving to experiment with, the load side is not.
- This exact pattern, microcontroller plus relay plus WiFi, is the core idea behind most smart plugs and smart light switches on the market.

lesson.summary: Swapping a plain digitalRead() for **analogRead()** lets your microcontroller respond to a range of brightness, not just on or off.
lesson.content:
## Project: A Light-Sensitive Night Light

> **Core Concept:** Swapping a plain digitalRead() for **analogRead()** lets your microcontroller respond to a range of brightness, not just on or off.

### Why It Matters
- Every project so far treated the world as binary, pressed or not pressed, triggered or not. Real light levels are a gradient, and this project is the first to actually measure one.
- It introduces a **photoresistor (LDR)** and a **voltage divider**, the standard way to turn a changing resistance into a changing voltage a microcontroller can read.
- It's also the first project with a genuinely useful, always-on purpose: an LED that quietly takes care of itself as it gets dark.

### Intuitive Analogy
A photoresistor is like a person who only complains loudly when a room
gets genuinely dark, staying quiet the rest of the time. Instead of a
button giving you a clean yes or no, the photoresistor's resistance
slides smoothly from low (bright) to high (dark), and the microcontroller
reads that sliding scale, then decides for itself where "dark enough"
starts.


### Key Engineering Principles
- Parts needed: one LED, one resistor for the LED, one photoresistor (LDR), one fixed resistor (around 10k ohm) to form a voltage divider, jumper wires, breadboard.
- Voltage divider wiring: 5V through the LDR, then down through the fixed resistor to ground, with the midpoint (between the two) connected to an analog input pin.
- As the room gets darker, the LDR's resistance **rises**, which shifts the voltage at that midpoint, and analogRead() picks up that shift as a changing number. A voltage divider is the standard trick for turning any resistance change into a voltage change, it shows up constantly beyond just LDRs.
- analogRead() returns a value from **0 to 1023** on most boards (a 10-bit reading), not just HIGH or LOW like digitalRead(). That range comes from the board's analog-to-digital converter, which slices the voltage between 0V and its reference voltage into 1024 discrete steps.
- In code, pick a **threshold** number by testing your actual room, then compare the analogRead() result against it each pass through loop().
- When the reading crosses into 'dark' territory, drive the LED pin HIGH, and when it's bright again, drive it LOW.
- Which resistor sits on top and which sits on bottom in the divider matters. ==Swap the LDR and fixed resistor's positions== and the midpoint voltage moves the opposite direction as light changes, quietly inverting your whole threshold logic.
- The exact threshold number isn't a universal constant, it depends on the specific LDR's resistance range, the fixed resistor's value, and the room's actual lighting, which is why **testing beats guessing** here.
- This voltage-divider pattern generalizes: swap the LDR for almost any resistance-based sensor (a flex sensor, a force sensor, a thermistor) and the same wiring and analogRead() approach still applies.

lesson.summary: A line-following robot just compares two **IR sensor** readings and steers by giving the motor on the wrong side more or less power.
lesson.content:
## Project: Line-Following Robot Basics

> **Core Concept:** A line-following robot just compares two **IR sensor** readings and steers by giving the motor on the wrong side more or less power.

### Why It Matters
- This project is the simplest real example of a robot making its own decisions from sensor data instead of running a fixed script.
- It combines two sensors and two actuators around one brain for the first time, which is the shape of almost every real robotics project.
- Understanding this basic logic is what makes fancier line-following, with more sensors or smoother turning, make sense later.

### Intuitive Analogy
Picture walking along a painted line on a sidewalk with your eyes closed,
except you have one finger on each side of the line brushing the ground.
If your left finger feels the dark line and your right one feels plain
pavement, you know you've drifted left of center and need to nudge right,
and the reverse if it's your right finger that finds the line. Two simple
sensors, one on each side, is really all it takes to keep a robot roughly
centered on a line.


### Key Engineering Principles
- Parts needed: two IR (infrared) reflectance sensors, two DC motors with a motor driver, wheels and a simple chassis, and your microcontroller board.
- IR sensors detect the line by reflected light, dark surfaces (the line) reflect less infrared light back than light surfaces (the floor), so the sensor outputs a digital HIGH or LOW depending on which it sees.
- Each IR sensor module actually contains both an infrared emitter and a separate infrared receiver, mounted side by side, the emitter shines light down and the receiver measures how much bounces back.
- Wiring: each IR sensor's output goes to its own digital input pin, each motor connects through the driver to its own PWM-capable output pin, and both motors share the driver's common power and ground connections.
- Core logic: read both sensors, and if both see floor, drive both motors forward at the same speed to go straight down the line's path.
- If the left sensor sees the line, slow down or stop the left motor and keep the right motor going, turning the robot left back toward center, and mirror that logic for the right sensor, this is the entire steering algorithm.
- Keeping this loop running continuously, read sensors then adjust motors then repeat, is what makes the robot 'follow' the line rather than just react once, corrections happen many times per second.
- Sensor placement and spacing matters a lot, sensors mounted too close together ==barely react before the robot has already drifted off the line==, and sensors mounted too far apart overreact to small wiggles.
- The height of the sensors above the floor affects reliability too, IR reflectance sensors typically work best within a specific narrow range, often around 3 to 10 millimeters, specified by the sensor's own datasheet.
- This basic two-sensor, two-motor design is a **bang-bang controller**, it only has two states per side (full correction or none), more advanced versions use **proportional control**, adjusting speed gradually based on how far off-center the robot is instead of a hard on/off switch.

topics.description: **PWM** lets a microcontroller control a motor's speed by rapidly switching full power on and off, not by lowering the voltage.

lesson.summary: **PWM** lets a microcontroller control a motor's speed by rapidly switching full power on and off, not by lowering the voltage.
lesson.content:
## Project: Motor Speed Control

> **Core Concept:** **PWM** lets a microcontroller control a motor's speed by rapidly switching full power on and off, not by lowering the voltage.

### Why It Matters
- A GPIO pin ==can't safely drive a motor directly==, and simply turning it on and off gives you only two speeds: full and stopped.
- Real projects need smooth speed control, like a fan that ramps up or a robot that eases into a turn.
- This project connects two ideas you've already seen, **PWM** signals and using a switch-style driver, into one working, adjustable motor.

### Intuitive Analogy
Think of PWM speed control like flicking a light switch on and off faster
than your eye can follow. If it's on 80 percent of the time and off 20
percent, the light looks dimmer, even though it's always either fully on
or fully off. A motor works the same way: pulsing full power on and off
very fast makes it spin slower or faster depending on how much of each
pulse is "on" time, without ever asking the motor to run on a reduced
voltage.


### Key Engineering Principles
- Parts needed: a small DC motor, a motor driver module (like an L298N, or a single transistor/MOSFET setup), a flyback diode if your driver doesn't already include one, and a separate power source for the motor.
- Never wire a motor's power leads directly to a GPIO pin, a **motor driver** sits between the microcontroller and the motor to safely handle the higher current a motor draws, especially at startup.
- Wiring: microcontroller's PWM-capable pin to the driver's input (or enable) pin, driver's output to the motor, and the motor's own power supply to the driver, keeping motor power separate from the board's logic power.
- In code, **analogWrite()** sends a PWM signal with a **duty cycle** value from 0 (off) to 255 (full speed) instead of a plain HIGH or LOW, and the driver amplifies that signal into real motor current.
- Ramping the analogWrite() value up gradually, instead of jumping straight to a target speed, gives a smoother start instead of a sudden jolt and reduces the current spike the motor demands at the instant it starts spinning.
- This builds directly on the same PWM idea used to dim an LED, the only real difference is a motor driver stands between the pin and the higher-current motor, since a motor draws far more current than an LED ever would.
- A DC motor is **inductive**, meaning it stores energy in a magnetic field while running. When power to it is suddenly cut, that stored energy has to go somewhere, and it discharges as a brief high-voltage spike, which is exactly what the flyback diode exists to redirect safely.
- The flyback diode is wired backward relative to normal current flow through the motor, so it does nothing while the motor runs normally, and only conducts when that shutoff voltage spike tries to push current the wrong way.
- Motor drivers like the L298N usually provide two logic inputs per motor for direction plus one PWM enable input for speed, which is what lets a single driver handle both forward/reverse and variable speed together.
- ==Stalling a motor==, blocking it from turning while power is still applied, makes it draw far more current than normal since a stopped motor has almost no **back-EMF** resisting the current, which is a common way to overheat a driver or motor.

topics.title: Project: RGB Mood Lamp
topics.description: Mixing **PWM** brightness across a red, green, and blue LED lets one lamp produce almost any color you want, entirely in code.

lesson.summary: Mixing **PWM** brightness across a red, green, and blue LED lets one lamp produce almost any color you want, entirely in code.
lesson.content:
## Project: RGB Mood Lamp

> **Core Concept:** Mixing **PWM** brightness across a red, green, and blue LED lets one lamp produce almost any color you want, entirely in code.

### Why It Matters
- This project is the clearest hands-on proof that PWM isn't just for motors and dimming, it's also how digital color mixing actually works.
- It turns three separate output pins into one flexible, programmable light source instead of three fixed-color LEDs.
- Cycling colors automatically is a satisfying, visible way to practice loops and timing in code.

### Intuitive Analogy
Think of a stage light crew mixing colored spotlights on a single spot.
Full red and full blue together with no green makes a bold magenta. Dial
the red down and the blue up and the color shifts smoothly. An RGB LED is
really just three tiny spotlights, red, green, and blue, crammed behind
one lens, and PWM is the dimmer knob for each one.


### Key Engineering Principles
- Parts needed: one RGB LED (common cathode is easiest for beginners), three current-limiting resistors (one per color), jumper wires, and a breadboard.
- An RGB LED is really three separate LED dies in one package, each with its own leg, plus one shared leg (common cathode or common anode) that ties all three together internally.
- Wiring: each of the LED's red, green, and blue legs goes through its own resistor to its own PWM-capable output pin, and the common leg goes to ground (for a common cathode LED). Never share a single resistor across two color legs, each one needs its own.
- In code, three separate analogWrite() calls, one per color pin, each with its own 0-255 brightness value, set the mixed color, exactly like dimming three independent LEDs at once.
- Full brightness on all three (255, 255, 255) makes white, all zero makes the LED off, and every other combination blends toward a different hue, this is additive color mixing, the same principle behind how screens produce color.
- To cycle colors automatically, store several color combinations, for example as three small arrays or a list of RGB triples, and move to the next one every second or two using delay().
- Keep resistor values appropriate for each color, red, green, and blue LED dies often have different forward voltages even inside the same package, commonly around 2V for red and closer to 3V for green and blue, so a single resistor value chosen for one color may run another too dim or too bright.
- ==Human eyes don't perceive brightness linearly==, doubling a PWM value doesn't look twice as bright, it looks like a smaller jump than that, which is why smooth color fades sometimes look uneven near the low end unless you compensate with a **gamma correction** curve.
- A common cathode LED's shared leg goes to ground and each color leg is driven HIGH-ish (via PWM) to light it, a common anode LED works the opposite way, its shared leg goes to the positive supply and each color leg is driven LOW-ish (via inverted PWM) to light it.
- Beyond simple color cycling, RGB brightness values can be driven by a sensor (like a potentiometer or a microphone module) instead of a fixed list, turning this into a mood lamp that reacts to its environment rather than repeating a script.

topics.title: Project: A Simple Alarm
topics.description: An alarm is just a **sensor input** wired to an **alert output**, with code in between deciding when 'triggered' actually means triggered.

lesson.summary: An alarm is just a **sensor input** wired to an **alert output**, with code in between deciding when 'triggered' actually means triggered.
lesson.content:
## Project: A Simple Alarm

> **Core Concept:** An alarm is just a **sensor input** wired to an **alert output**, with code in between deciding when 'triggered' actually means triggered.

### Why It Matters
- This project shifts the goal from 'make a light blink' to 'detect a real event and respond immediately', which is what most sensor-based projects actually do.
- It reuses the digitalRead() skill from the button project, but now the input represents something happening in the world, not a deliberate press.
- A buzzer is a new kind of output: instead of light, it's sound, and it's wired almost exactly like an LED.

### Intuitive Analogy
Think of this like a simple home alarm system, minus the monthly
subscription. There's a sensor watching for one specific condition (a
door opening, a tilt, a beam breaking), and the moment that condition is
true, the system doesn't debate it or wait, it immediately makes noise.
Your microcontroller is playing the part of that instant, no-second-guessing
response.


### Key Engineering Principles
- Parts needed: a trigger sensor (a pushbutton, a tilt switch, or a light sensor all work), a small buzzer or LED as the alert, a resistor if using an LED, jumper wires, breadboard.
- Wiring the sensor: for a button or tilt switch, one side to 5V, the other side to an input pin and to ground through a pull-down resistor, same pattern as the button project.
- Wiring the buzzer: one leg to an output pin, the other leg to ground, no resistor needed for most small active buzzers, since they contain their own internal driver circuit rather than behaving like a bare LED.
- In code, pinMode() sets the sensor pin as INPUT and the buzzer pin as OUTPUT.
- loop() constantly reads the sensor, and the instant it reads triggered, drives the buzzer pin HIGH.
- A short delay() after triggering keeps the alarm sounding for a beat instead of cutting off the instant the sensor reading flickers.
- A tilt switch is really just a switch with a small internal ball or blob of conductive material that bridges its two contacts only at certain angles, electrically it behaves exactly like a pushbutton once it's closed.
- **Active buzzers** take a plain HIGH or LOW and produce one fixed tone on their own. **Passive buzzers** instead need a changing signal, like tone(), to actually produce sound, ==feeding a passive buzzer a plain HIGH just makes a faint click or nothing at all==.
- **Debouncing**, briefly ignoring a sensor reading right after it changes, matters more here than in the earlier button project, since a mechanical tilt switch can chatter for a few milliseconds right at the trigger moment and you don't want that read as multiple separate events.
